tracks.title: A disk that rides in the file
tracks.text: Lesson nine — the VFS. The virtual file system is the workbook's own disk. Real files and directories, SQLite-backed… riding inside the artifact. [curious] The workspace your code and your agents work in is the same file you can send. And nothing they do can touch the computer it's sitting on.

tracks.title: Where does an agent keep files?
tracks.text: Give software somewhere to work, and you've answered most of what it needs. The industry's answer for agents has been one of two bad options. Option one: hand over your real disk. Your keychain… your documents… everything a bad instruction can reach. Option two: rent a computer in the cloud, metered by the second — so the agent has a scratch directory that evaporates when the meter stops. [curious] Both answers share an assumption worth questioning… that a file system has to belong to a machine. Yours, or someone else's. But the amount of disk a project actually needs is small. And what it needs from that disk is mundane. Paths… directories… read, write, list. Nothing about that requires an operating system underneath. So the missing piece isn't a bigger disk, or a cheaper rental. [excited] It's a disk that belongs to the project — one that travels when the project travels.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. The VFS is the workbook's own disk. A virtual file system — real files and directories, SQLite-backed — riding inside the artifact. Readable and writable by the workbook's code and agents… and sealed off from the host machine, by construction. It's the third layer of the workbook anatomy. The interface up front… WebAssembly for compute… and underneath them, a disk. [curious] So the file doesn't just describe a piece of software. It contains the place where that software keeps its things.

tracks.title: A disk you can query
tracks.text: Under the paths, the VFS is tables. And that duality is the feature. To the code, it's a disk — open, read, write, list, like any file system. To a query, it's SQLite — the same bytes, askable. [curious] Most file systems make you choose… easy paths, or real queries. Because this one is a database wearing a directory tree, the painful questions become single statements. Everything modified since the last deploy? One select… six rows. Where do the megabytes actually live? One select — the assets directory, eleven megabytes, and everything else is a rounding error. Every file the agent touched this week? One select… fourteen rows — its notes, two drafts, one finished report. Try asking your operating system that second question. There's a progress bar involved. Here, a listing was never a crawl in the first place. It was always a query. [chuckles] Your disk speaks SQL.

tracks.title: What's actually inside
tracks.text: So what's actually inside the store? Three kinds of thing, and none of them exotic. First… paths. The namespace — a table of names that makes slash notes slash june dot org mean something. Second… blobs. The bytes themselves, one per file, sitting in the same store. And third… metadata. Sizes, times, who wrote what — as columns, not as a cache your tools rebuild by crawling. Directories deserve a sentence of their own. On a normal disk, the question of what belongs to this project is answered by folklore — a naming convention, an ignore file, a readme that says don't touch the vendor folder. Here, a directory is a fact in a table… and what's in this tree is an answer you select, not an answer you reconstruct. And the door swings both ways. Unbundle a workbook, and the tree unpacks to ordinary files on your real disk. The store itself is plain SQLite — readable by the most widely deployed database tooling on earth. The format holds your files. It doesn't hold them hostage.

tracks.title: Two readings, again
tracks.text: The workbook lesson describes one file with two readings — a document to a human, a container to an engine. The VFS is where that duality becomes concrete. Opened in a browser… the VFS loads into memory. Code reads and writes it for real — a game saves, a dashboard filters, an agent's notes are right there. And when you close the tab, the file on your disk is exactly what it was. The artifact stays honest. Viewing never mutates. [curious] Docked into a Nexus… the same VFS becomes the workbook's live disk. Persistent. Synced. Served. Writes survive restarts… schedules write into it overnight… and the copy you serve to a thousand people reads from it. Same paths. Same queries. Same code. It's one promise with two tenses. In the browser, the disk is a reading — fully real while you're there, gone without a trace when you leave. On the engine, it's a residence. [excited] The only thing that changed is that the disk now has a heartbeat.

tracks.title: The workspace is the artifact
tracks.text: Here's the consequence that makes this construct worth its own lesson. An agent's working directory — its notes, its drafts, its intermediate data, its memory — lives in the VFS of the workbook it's tending. Which means the workspace, and the work product… are the same object. Hand someone the file, and you've handed them the project. The app… its data… and the entire working state of the agents that built it. No zipping up a folder. No it-works-on-my-sandbox. This is also what makes handoffs between humans and agents boring, in the good way. There's no export step where context dies. The agent's scratch files and decision notes sit in slash notes, right next to the deliverable in slash reports — and whoever opens the file next starts from the real state, not a summary of it. [excited] The thing you collaborate on and the thing you ship… stopped being different things.

tracks.title: A day in the life
tracks.text: Abstractions should earn their keep — so here's one ordinary day in the life of one workbook's disk. Six in the morning. A schedule fires on the engine, an agent runs its workflow, pulls the week's orders out of slash data, and writes the finished report to slash reports — a path that didn't exist a minute earlier. Nine o'clock. You open the served workbook with your coffee, and the dashboard's chart is a live query against the path the agent wrote three hours ago. Nothing was uploaded, deployed, or synced… because the disk the agent wrote and the disk the dashboard reads were never two disks. Eleven. Your accountant asks for the numbers. She does not want a login. You unbundle one file out of the VFS and email her an ordinary CSV. [curious] Now ask — which machine's disk did all of that touch? … Not yours. Your laptop could have been closed in a bag the whole time. That's the whole pitch, wearing a Tuesday.

tracks.title: Why this is the safe shape
tracks.text: Now — why this is the safe shape. An agent that needs your file system is an agent you have to trust with your file system. An agent whose entire disk is the VFS needs no trust at all. Every write it makes — even a confused one — lands in the VFS. Your documents… your keychain… the OS disk — no path resolves to any of them. The only door out is a specific, revocable grant — the grants-not-inheritance rule, starting here. Then the part people underestimate: prompt injection. Anyone whose text reaches your agent is partially steering it. Give a steerable agent your operating system, and you've built an exfiltration machine with a stranger near the wheel. [curious] Give it a VFS… and the same hostile instruction hits a wall made of construction, not policy. The worst text can do is trash one project-sized disk. And even that is boring — the disk lives inside a file git was tracking all along. A bad week: Tuesday… version one ships. Wednesday… the agent writes reports. Thursday… a bad write trashes the data. Thirty seconds later — one git revert, disk restored. [chuckles] Versioned, diffable, restorable… because files already have the best undo humanity ever shipped.

tracks.title: Four places to keep bytes
tracks.text: It's worth lining the disk up against its alternatives, honestly. Project bytes live in one of four places today. Your operating system's disk… which nobody can query, and which is the host — sandboxing from it is the whole problem. A cloud bucket… durable, sure, but it doesn't travel with the project — the project just points at it, and the meter for storage and egress never stops. A rented sandbox volume… properly isolated, and gone when the rental ends. [curious] And then the VFS — the only one of the four that travels with the work, answers SQL, is sealed from the host by construction, and gets versioned for free, because it lives inside a file git was already tracking. The honest read: the other three still exist for reasons, at your system's boundaries. A bucket is the right home for a terabyte of video. But each of them wins one column and forfeits the rest… and the VFS is the only one whose virtue is the project's coherence itself.

tracks.title: Where the disk ends
tracks.text: Honesty section. The VFS is a project-scale disk… not a media vault. SQLite holds gigabytes comfortably, but a workbook stays pleasant to share in the tens of megabytes — so heavy assets belong behind an engine, with the workbook querying them. Put the catalog in the file… and the warehouse behind the Nexus. And in a browser, persistence is the file's. Changes live in memory until you save, or dock. The open tab is a reading room… not a writing desk. That's a designed property, not a gap — it's what makes opening a stranger's workbook safe. [curious] But it means the browser alone is not where durable state accumulates. For durability, schedules, and serving — the engine is the answer. The way it always is, for the living part.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Are they real files, or files in quotation marks? Real, to everything inside. Code opens paths… agents list directories… tools read and write bytes. Your OS sees one file. The workbook sees a disk. Can I get files out? Always — unbundle, and the tree unpacks to ordinary files. What happens to the VFS when I email the file? It goes along. The disk is bytes in the html, so sending the file sends the disk — and the recipient opens the same paths with no setup. Can code inside list MY computer's files? No. And not because a setting says no — there is no path that resolves outside the artifact, so escaping to the host disk isn't a permission to deny… it's a sentence with no referent. What about two people writing at once? That's a docked question — the engine holds the live VFS and serializes the writes. And why SQLite underneath? Same reason as the rest of the anatomy. No invented formats… just what existing ingredients do when they share a file.

tracks.title: Wrapping up
tracks.text: So that's the VFS. A real disk, riding in the artifact — queryable like a database, sealed off from the host, versioned with the work, and identical in the browser and on the engine. The workspace is the work product… and an entire Tuesday can happen on a disk no machine of yours had to hold. That idea echoes through every other lesson… [excited] go meet its neighbors.
